sec.title: Background
sec.p: Honey is a natural product with a complex chemical composition and beneficial effects on human health. The floral or honeydew origin of honey determines its compositional diversity, thereby affecting its bioactivity and associated health outcomes. This study comparatively evaluates the antioxidant, antigenotoxic, and antimicrobial properties of five honey types: honeydew, meadow, wild cherry, sunflower, and acacia.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Melissopalynological analysis was used to confirm honeys’ botanical or honeydew origins. Chemical profiles of honey samples, as well as their antioxidant activity via 2,2-diphenylpicrylhydrazyl (DPPH), 2,2’-azino-bis-3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid (ABTS) and total reducing power (TRP) assays were determined. Antigenotoxicity was assessed using both in vitro and in vivo models, while antimicrobial activity was evaluated against eight microbial strains.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The results demonstrated that honeydew and meadow honeys had the highest total phenolic content (TPC), as well as superior antioxidant activity in DPPH and TRP assays, while wild cherry, sunflower, and acacia honeys showed stronger ABTS radical scavenging. All honey samples significantly reduced DNA damage induced by hydroxyl and peroxyl radicals in vitro. Acacia honey displayed the highest in vivo DNA-protective activity, followed by meadow and honeydew samples. Likewise, all honey types showed good antimicrobial activity, especially meadow honey.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: These findings suggest that the tested honey samples exhibit bioactive properties and support their further investigation in the context of human health.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: As a natural substance, honey has been used throughout history in traditional medicine and nutrition. It is produced by honey bees (genus Apis) through the enzymatic processing of floral nectar and honeydew, but also by other bee genera, including stingless bees. Nectar-derived honey is categorized as either monofloral, when it is mostly generated from a single plant species, or polyfloral, when it is derived from the nectar of diverse plant sources. In contrast, honeydew honey is obtained by metabolic processing of plant secretions or the excretions of phloem-feeding insects [1–4].

Honey represents a natural source of sugars, enzymes, vitamins, minerals and other bioactive compounds which not only serve as relevant dietary components but also contribute to its health-promoting properties [5]. The preventive and therapeutic potentials of honey in human health are mostly attributed to its antioxidant [6], anti-inflammatory [7], antimutagenic [8, 9], antigenotoxic [10, 11], antiviral [12], antimicrobial [13, 14] and other functional properties. These biological activities support honey’s possible implication in the prevention and treatment of numerous pathological conditions [5, 15]. Many human diseases are caused by oxidative damage induced by free radicals. Therefore, in addition to endogenous production of antioxidants, their dietary intake is also desirable, and honey is well known for being rich in antioxidant compounds [6, 16]. As well as, owing to its antigenotoxic properties, honey may exert a preventive effect against the harmful action of environmental genotoxic agents, such as irinotecan and hydrogen peroxide [10, 11]. In addition, its application has been associated with improved wound repair and tissue regeneration [3, 4, 7, 17]. Thanks to its prebiotic effects, honey can support the balance of gut microbiota, decrease inflammation, and improve general health [18]. As many bacteria are becoming resistant to antibiotics, honey may serve as a complementary therapy that helps in suppression of persistent strains [13]. The diverse array of bioactive effects observed in honey arises from its complex composition [4, 17, 19], whereby its bioactive compounds, such as polyphenols, vitamins, minerals, enzymes and others, contribute to its classification as a functional food that provides health benefits beyond basic nutrition [5, 19, 20].

However, the representation of bioactive constituents in honey is influenced, among others, by botanical and honeydew origins. The plant species from which bees collect nectar or honeydew directly determine its chemical composition, including phenolic content, antioxidant potential, and antimicrobial activity [4, 19, 21]. In this context, the purpose of the present work was to investigate the antioxidant, antigenotoxic, and antimicrobial properties of five honey types obtained from different sources: honeydew honey (HH), meadow honey (MH), wild cherry honey (WCH), sunflower honey (SH), and acacia honey (ACH).

sec.title: Honey samples
sec.p: We have examined five different raw honey samples (Table 1), collected between 2019 and 2023, which were obtained from beekeepers directly. The honey samples were obtained from stationary apiaries located at a single geographic location, ensuring consistent environmental conditions during honey production. The artificial honey (AH) used as a control sample was prepared by dissolving 40 g fructose, 30 g glucose, 8 g maltose, and 2 g sucrose in 100 ml of distilled water, followed by filtration through a 0.22 μm syringe membrane filter (Membrane Solutions, Auburn, WA, USA) [22].

sec.title: Melissopalynological screening of honey samples
sec.p: A provisional melissopalynological screening was conducted to confirm the botanical origin of the honey samples. Honey samples (10 g) were dissolved in 50 mL of distilled water and centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 15 min. The sediment was washed and centrifuged again under identical conditions [23]. Acetolysis was not performed, and the resulting pellet was mounted in glycerin–gelatin medium containing basic fuchsin (Gelatin-Fuchsin) and examined using light microscopy.

For each honey sample, three independent microscope slides were prepared, and pollen grains were examined using ×10, ×20, and ×40 objective magnifications. Identification of pollen types was based on morphological characteristics such as size, shape, aperture type, and exine ornamentation [24], using standard atlases and the PalDat pollen database. A rapid pollen assessment was performed as an estimate analysis according to the classification of Louveaux et al. to identify diagnostic pollen types and verify whether the analyzed honey samples met the criteria prescribed by the Serbian national regulation „Rulebook on Quality and Other Requirements for Honey, Other Bee Products, Preparations Based on Honey and Other Bee Products“ (Official Gazette of Serbia and Montenegro, No. 45/2003) [24, 25]. The estimate analysis included counting 100 pollen grains per slide. AH served as a negative control to verify the absence of pollen contamination during sample preparation. All slides were imaged using a Leica binocular microscope DFC 320 (M2 16 A) (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany).

sec.title: Determination of the chemical profile of honey samples
Chemicals
sec.p: 2,2′-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH), Folin–Ciocalteu’s phenol reagent, iron (III) chloride, sodium carbonate, trichloro acetic acid were purchased by Merck (Darmstadt, Germany). 6-Hydroxy-2,5,7,8-tetramethylchroman-2-carboxylic acid (Trolox) was purchased from Acros Organics (Morris Plains, NJ, USA). Solutions were prepared using deionized water (specific conductivity 0.05 µS/cm) which was produced using MicroMed high purity water systems (TKA Wasseraufbereitungsysteme GmbH, Niederelbert, Germany).

sec.title: Determination of free acidity and pH
sec.p: Free acidity was determined by titrimetric method using a solution containing 10 g of honey dissolved in 75 mL of distilled water, at room temperature [26]. The solution was titrated with 0.1 mol/L NaOH to pH 8.5. The result was expressed in milliequivalents (meq) of acid per kg of honey (meq/kg).

A 20% w/v honey solution was used to determine the pH value, at 25 °C. A SevenDirect SD20 pH meter (Mettler Toledo, Urdorf, Switzerland) was used to measure the pH value. Before each measurement, the electrode was calibrated using pH standards of 4.01 ± 0.02 and 7.01 ± 0.02 [27].

sec.title: Determination of dry matter and ash content
sec.p: The dry matter content was determined using a 2WAJ OPTICA Microscopes refractometer. A few drops of honey were placed on the prism of the refractometer and the result was read directly from the display [26].

Ash content was determined according to the AOAC [26] method. A honey sample (5 g) was weighed, combusted and heated at high temperature (550 °C) for 5 h. After cooling to room temperature, the resulting ash content was measured on an analytical balance and results were presented as % of ash.

sec.title: Determination of sugar content
sec.p: Identification and quantification of the sugars were performed using an Agilent 1200 Series HPLC, equipped with auto-sampler injector, quaternary pump, degasser and refractive index detector (RID), previously described by Trajković et al. [28]. Honey samples were prepared by dissolving honey in deionized water (20% w/v). In brief, 20 µL of honey samples was injected and elution of was performed in isocratic mode on the ZORBAX (Agilent) NH2 column, 5 μm (4.5 mm × 250 mm). The column was thermostated at 23 °C with a flow rate of 1 mL/min of mobile phase MeCN and water (75:25). The temperature of the RID was 35 °C. The chromatographic peaks were identified by comparing the retention time of the injected standard solution against the constituents of the honey samples. Quantification was performed based on calibration curves of each identified sugar.

sec.title: Determination of total phenolic content (TPC)
sec.p: Total phenolic content (TPC) of honey samples was determined using Folin–Cicoalteu assay [29]. Briefly, 50 µL of diluted honey samples (20% w/v) was mixed with 20% solution of Na2CO3, followed by addition of Folin–Cicoalteu and water. Gallic acid was used to construct calibration curve. Blanks were run to correct absorbance, and a positive control (standard solution at a mid-range concentration) was measured to verify assay performance across runs. Absorbances of obtained mixtures were measured at 750 nm after 30 min in the dark and the results were expressed as µg gallic acid equivalents (GAE) per 1 mg of sample (µg GAE/mg). All measurements were performed in triplicate and results were expressed as mean ± SD.

sec.title: The 2,2-diphenylpicrylhydrazyl (DPPH) assay
sec.p: The 2,2-diphenylpicrylhydrazyl (DPPH) assay method was performed by mixing 100 µL solution of honey samples with 1.5 mL of DPPH radical solution and diluted to final volume of 4 mL using methanol [29]. Trolox was used to construct calibration curve. Blanks were run to correct absorbance, and a positive control (standard solution at a mid-range concentration) was measured to verify assay performance across runs. Obtained mixtures were left to stand in the dark for 1 h, and after that absorbances were recorded at 515 nm. Results were expressed as µg of Trolox equivalents (TE) per 1 mg of honey (µg TE/mg). All measurements were performed in triplicate and results were expressed as mean ± SD.

sec.title: The 2,2’-azino-bis-3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid (ABTS) assay
sec.p: In the 2,2’-azino-bis-3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid (ABTS) assay, the ABTS radical was produced by the reaction of ABTS stock with potassium persulfate and the mixture was allowed to stand in the dark at 25 °C for 12 − 16 h before use to obtain ABTS·+ solution [30]. An aliquot (100 µL) of honey samples solution was mixed with 1.8 mL of diluted ABTS·+ solution at the concentration and diluted with methanol to a total volume of 4 mL. After 6 min at 25 °C, the reduction in absorbance was measured at 734 nm. Trolox was used to construct calibration curve. Blanks were run to correct absorbance, and a positive control (standard solution at a mid-range concentration) was measured to verify assay performance across runs. Results were expressed as µg of Trolox equivalents (TE) per 1 mg of honey (µg TE/mg). All measurements were performed in triplicate and results were expressed as mean ± SD.

sec.title: Total reducing power (TRP)
sec.p: Total reducing power (TRP) was estimated using a method previously described by Mitić et al. [30]. Reaction mixtures were prepared by mixing aliquot (10 µL) of honey solution, 1% solution K3[Fe(CN)6], phosphate buffer (pH 6.6) and water. The mixtures were incubated at 50 °C for 30 min and then 10% solution of trichloroacetic acid and FeCl3 were added. Acorbic acid was used to construct calibration curve. Blanks were run to correct absorbance, and a positive control (standard solution at a mid-range concentration) was measured to verify assay performance across runs. Results were expressed as µg ascorbic acid equivalents (AAE) per 1 mg of sample (µg AAE/mg). All measurements were performed in triplicate and results were expressed as mean ± SD.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed using Statistica 8.0 software, (StatSoft, Tulsa, Oklahoma, USA). The paired Student t-test was used to compare the characteristics of different samples at a probability level of p < 0.05, as statistically significant.

sec.title: Chemicals
sec.p: Phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) without calcium and magnesium, normal melting point agarose (NMA), low melting point agarose (LMA), and collagenase were obtained from Alfatrade Enterprise D.O.O. Salmon sperm DNA sodium salt was purchased from Carl Roth (GmbH, Karlsruhe, Germany) and ethyl methanesulphonate (EMS) was from Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA. All other chemicals were purchased from local suppliers in Serbia (including Alfamed d.o.o., Unichem d.o.o., and Promedia d.o.o.) and were of analytical reagent grade.

sec.title: Fly strain
sec.p: The fly and larvae of wild-type strain Oregon-R-C of Drosophila melanogaster (Bloomington Indiana University, USA) were cultured in glass bottles at a temperature of 25 °C, relative humidity of about 60% and in a 12/12 h light/dark regime on standard corn medium containing agar, sugar, yeast and fungicide.

sec.title: Assessment of in vitro antigenotoxic activity
sec.p: The antigenotoxic potential of the honey samples was evaluated by examining their ability to protect DNA from oxidative damage caused by hydroxyl and peroxyl radicals. Three concentrations of honey (1, 10, and 20%) were tested using salmon sperm DNA sodium salt as an in vitro model [31, 32], while quercetin (100 µg/mL) served as a reference antioxidant [33]. To prepare the test samples, the required concentrations of honey were initially dissolved in methanol, which was subsequently removed by complete evaporation. The reaction mixtures were then assembled by adding 45 µL of phosphate buffer (0.2 M, pH 7.4) and 10 µL of salmon sperm DNA (10 mg/mL in 0.9% NaCl) to the honey samples or the standard compound.

Oxidative DNA damage mediated by hydroxyl radicals was induced by the addition of FeSO₄ (0.9 µL, 180 mM) and H₂O₂ (3.6 µL, 600 mM). Following a 15 min incubation period, the reaction products were analyzed by electrophoresis on a 1% agarose gel prepared in 1× Tris–acetate–EDTA (TAE) buffer containing ethidium bromide (10 mg/mL).

For the generation of peroxyl radicals, 10 µL of 2,2’-azobis(2-amidinopropane) dihydrochloride (AAPH, 200 mM) was introduced into the reaction mixtures, which were then mixed and incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. After incubation, DNA samples were subjected to electrophoretic separation under the same conditions as described above.

Gel images were recorded using a UV transilluminator (Vilber Lourmat, France) operating at 365 nm, and the extent of DNA protection was quantified by densitometric analysis using ImageJ software (version 1.48, Softonic International, Barcelona, Spain). The extent of DNA damage was expressed as relative DNA band intensity compared to the negative control.

sec.title: Assessment of in vivo antigenotoxic activity
sec.p: For the negative control, third instar larvae of D. melanogaster (74 ± 2 h) were placed in a standard Drosophila corn medium prepared with PBS. For positive control, the larvae were transferred to a medium with EMS (1 mM in PBS). For the evaluation of antigenotoxicity, larvae were placed in a medium with different concentrations of honey (1, 10, and 20%) and 1 mM EMS. After 24 h, treated larvae from each group (98 ± 2-h old) were removed from the media, and the cell suspension from the anterior midguts was prepared according to Howell and Taylor [34], modified by Mukhopadhyay et al. [35] and Siddique et al. [36].

The comet assay was performed according to Singh et al. [37] and Mukhopadhyay et al. [35]. The comets were visualized and captured with a ×40 objective lens of fluorescence microscope Nikon Ti-Eclipse, Wien, Austria attached to a CCD camera. By a visual scoring method [38] one hundred randomly selected cells (50 cells per two replicate slides) were analyzed per treatment and classified into five classes labelled as C0 (no or very low damage), C1, C2, C3 (low, medium and high DNA damage), and C4 (the highest level of DNA damage). The total comet score (TCS) was calculated by assigning each cell a DNA damage comet class from 0 to 4 and summing the scores according equation [39]: (% cells in class 0 × 0) + (% cells in class 1 × 1) + (% cells in class 2 × 2) + (% cells in class 3 × 3) + (% cells in class 4 × 4). The percentage reduction of DNA damage, indicating the antigenotoxic effect, was calculated relative to the positive control [40]: %R = TCSEMS − TCS honey + EMS /TCSEMS-TCSnegative control ×100.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Results were expressed as mean ± SD, and statistical evaluation of data was analyzed with one-way analysis (ANOVA) using SPSS statistical software package, version 13.0 for Windows. The significance level was set at p < 0.05.

sec.title: Microbial strains
sec.p: The antimicrobial activity of honey samples was determined against reference strains including three Gram-positive bacteria: Bacillus cereus ATCC 11778, Enterococcus faecalis ATCC 19433, Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 25923; four Gram-negative bacteria: Escherichia coli ATCC 25922, Klebsiella aerogenes ATCC 13048, Pseudomonas paraeruginosa ATCC 9027, Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Enteritidis ATCC 13076; and yeast Candida albicans ATCC 24433. Bacterial strains were cultured on Mueller-Hinton agar (Torlak, Belgrade, Serbia) at 37 °C, while yeast was grown on Sabouraud dextrose agar (Torlak, Belgrade, Serbia) at 30 °C.

sec.title: In vitro antimicrobial assay
sec.p: The micro/well dilution method was used to test the antimicrobial potential of honey samples following the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guideline [41] with modifications. Microbial suspensions were prepared from overnight cultures grown for 18–20 h at 37 °C on the appropriate agar plates described above. Bacterial suspensions were made in Mueller-Hinton broth (Torlak, Belgrade, Serbia), while yeast suspension was prepared in Sabouraud dextrose broth (Torlak, Belgrade, Serbia).

The final turbidity of the suspension was adjusted to O.5 McFarland using the McFarland densitometer (DEN-1B, Biosan, Riga, Latvia). Initial honey solutions were prepared in the appropriate nutritional broth (Mueller-Hinton broth for bacteria and Sabouraud dextrose broth for yeast) at a concentration of 500 mg/mL (50% w/v), and serial two-fold dilutions were performed in microtiter plates. Then, 100 µL of the initial or diluted honey solution was mixed with 90 µL of the corresponding broth and 10 µL of the prepared microbial suspension, resulting in final honey concentrations ranging from 250.00 to 0.1 mg/mL (25-0.01% v/v). For testing the antimicrobial activity of a 50% honey solution, the honey was dissolved in the appropriate broth at a concentration of 526 mg/mL. Then, 190 µL of this solution was mixed with 10 µL of microbial suspension. The microtiter plates were incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. After incubation, 20 µL of a 0.5% aqueous solution of triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) was added to wells containing bacterial strains, and color development indicated bacterial growth. Yeast growth was assessed visually, based on medium turbidity and sediment formation at the bottom of the wells. Ciprofloxacin (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was used as the positive control for antibacterial activity, while nystatin (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was the positive control for antifungal activity. Both antimicrobials were tested over a concentration range of 0.1-0.00005 mg/mL. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was defined as the lowest concentration of honey samples that inhibited visible microbial growth, indicated by color development for bacteria and by medium turbidity and sediment formation for yeast. The minimum microbicidal concentration (MMC) was determined by inoculating appropriate agar plates with broth cultures from each well that showed no visible growth and incubating them at suitable temperatures for 24 h. The MMC was identified as the lowest concentration of the honey samples, which resulted in 99.9% mortality of the tested microorganisms. All experiments were conducted in triplicate.

sec.title: Melissopalynological screening
sec.p: The melissopalynological screening of each honey sample revealed distinct microscopic characteristics that aligned with its anticipated floral or honeydew profile and supported its botanical origin (Fig. 1).

sec.p: The HH sample demonstrated very low pollen density (< 100 pollen grains per slide) and a predominance of non-pollen particulate material (honeydew element-to-pollen ratio greater than 2), such as fungal or sooty mold elements and resinous debris, which is consistent with a honeydew origin. The MH sample exhibited high pollen diversity and abundance, with no dominant pollen type, primarily consisting of tricolpate or tricolporate dicot pollen, with minimal debris, indicating a clear floral nectar source. The WCH sample contained > 45% Prunus avium pollen (threshold applied for the category “other monofloral honeys” [24]), identified by its triangular tricolporate morphology. The SH sample was characterized by the presence of diagnostic echinate Helianthus annuus pollen grains (> 20%), confirming its sunflower origin. The ACH sample contained Robinia pseudoacacia pollen (> 40%) alongside abundant Prunus-type pollen.
Overall, palynological observations supported the declared botanical origins for all samples.

sec.title: Chemical profile of honey samples
sec.p: The results revealed notable variation in acidity, pH, dry matter, and mineral content among the honey samples (Table 2). MH exhibited the highest dry matter content (98.75%) and acidity (0.0021 meq/kg), whereas SH showed the lowest pH (4.18) and dry matter content (80.15%). HH had the highest ash content (4.96%).

sec.title: Antioxidant properties of honey samples
sec.p: The antioxidant values determined using the DPPH and ABTS assays as well as TRP are summarized in Table 5. When comparing the analyzed honey samples, differences in antioxidant capacity were observed depending on the applied assay. Briefly, the DPPH assay revealed values ranging from 0.424 ± 0.003 µg TE/mg (HH) to 0.231 ± 0.003 µg TE/mg (WCH), while the ABTS assay indicated the highest value for ACH (0.0291 ± 0.0002 µg TE/mg) and the lowest for MH (0.0101 ± 0.0003 µg TE/mg). TRP values were the highest in MH and HH samples (0.062 ± 0.001 µg AAE/mg and 0.061 ± 0.002 µg AAE/mg, respectively), while the lowest in ACH sample (0.046 ± 0.001 µg AAE/mg).

sec.title: In vitro DNA protective effect of honey samples against oxidative damage induced by hydroxyl and peroxyl radicals
sec.p: The DNA protective effect of honey samples was evaluated in vitro against oxidative damage induced by hydroxyl and peroxyl radicals (Fig. 2). All samples demonstrated protective activity against radical-induced damage to salmon sperm DNA sodium salt, although a slight, sample-dependent decrease in efficacy was observed with increasing concentrations. MH and WCH samples demonstrated effective reduction of oxidative DNA damage induced by both hydroxyl and peroxyl radicals. HH, ACH, and control AH, had relatively stronger protective activity against peroxyl radical–induced DNA damage than against hydroxyl radical–induced damage. In contrast, the SH sample showed more effective reduction of oxidative DNA damage caused by hydroxyl radicals.

sec.title: In vivo protective effect of honey samples against EMS-induced genotoxicity in D. melanogaster
sec.p: The in vivo protective effect of honey samples against EMS-induced genotoxicity in third-instar larvae of D. melanogaster was assessed using an alkaline comet assay (Table 6). Treatment with EMS significantly increased (p < 0.05) the levels of DNA damage in the third instar larvae of D. melanogaster, with a total comet score of 125.30 ± 1.41, representing a 5.42-fold increase compared to the negative control. Co-treatment with three different concentrations of the HH sample and 1 mM EMS resulted in a statistically significant concentration-dependent reduction in total comet score compared to a positive control (62.80 ± 0.23, 51.32 ± 0.18, 40.21 ± 0.37, respectively, vs. 125.30 ± 1.41). Treatment with EMS and 20% MH sample showed a greater protective effect against EMS-induced DNA damage than the 1% concentration, with a percentage reduction of 84.24% and 68.65%, respectively. All concentrations of the WCH sample significantly reduced DNA damage compared to the positive control, with percentage reductions of 52.93, 61.25, and 69.80%, respectively. For the SH sample, larvae exposed at all tested concentrations exhibited significantly lower total comet scores compared to the positive control (66.22 ± 0.23, 59.42 ± 0.86, and 49.11 ± 0.93 vs. 125.30 ± 1.41). At 20% concentration, the ACH sample showed the greatest DNA protective effect, almost completely preventing EMS-induced DNA damage, with a percentage reduction of 91.76%. Although the control AH sample also reduced EMS-induced genotoxicity at all tested concentrations, the percentage reductions were less than 50% and were lower than those observed for the other honey samples. Across all honey treatments, the most frequently observed comet classes were 0, 1, and 2, while class 4 comets were not detected, while as expected, exposure to EMS alone resulted in the appearance of higher comet classes (3 and 4).

sec.title: Antimicrobial effect of honey samples
sec.p: The antimicrobial activity of honey samples against bacterial and yeast strains is shown in Table 7. MH had the best antimicrobial activity, inhibiting all tested strains, with MIC and MMC values in the range of 6.3–50.0%. The growth of the strains P. paraeruginosa and S. aureus was completely inhibited at concentrations of 6.3% and 12.5% respectively. SH also had good inhibitory activity against all tested strains with MIC values of 12.5% to 50.0%, while its microbicidal activity was much weaker with an MMC value of 50.0%. ACH inhibited the growth of all bacterial strains with MIC and MMC values in the range of 25.0–50.0% and 50.0%, respectively.

sec.p: The honey samples had a much weaker effect on C. albicans than on the bacterial strains. Only SH and MH showed inhibitory activity against yeast with MIC values of 25.0%. En. faecalis was the most resistant bacterial strain, and its growth was completely inhibited only by MH and HH at a concentration of 50.0%. B. cereus and S. aureus showed similar sensitivity to the antibacterial activity of the honey samples, but the MIC values of the honey samples that inhibited S. aureus were lower for HH and MH samples. Among the Gram-negative bacteria, K. aerogenes and E. coli were similarly sensitive, and their growth was affected by ACH, MH, and HH, with an MIC of less than 50%, while MH demonstrated the lowest MIC and MMC values (12.5% and 12.5% for K. aerogenes, 12.5% and 25.0% for E. coli). P. paraeruginosa was the most sensitive strain among the Gram-negative bacteria, with the MIC values ranging from 6.3% to 50.0%.

sec.title: Palynological screening
sec.p: Melissopalynological screening, in conjunction with physicochemical and sensory analyses, was conducted to determine the botanical origin of the honey samples and to verify labeling accuracy.

The HH sample demonstrated low pollen content and a predominance of honeydew-associated particles, which corresponded with elevated ash and phenolic values, both characteristic of honeydew honeys [42]. MH exhibited a diverse dicot pollen spectrum with minimal contaminants, confirming its polyfloral origin. SH and WCH contained diagnostic pollen morphologies for Helianthus annuus and Prunus avium, respectively, thereby validating their botanical authenticity [43]. The ACH sample contained Robinia pseudoacacia pollen, alongside a significant portion of Prunus-type grains. This finding aligns with the known low pollen yield and under-representation of Robinia pollen in acacia honeys [44]. In conjunction with its high fructose content and low phenolic profile, these observations support the accurate classification of the ACH sample as acacia honey [45].
Overall, the palynological findings were consistent with the chemical and sensory analyses, reinforcing the reliability of the sample classifications.

sec.title: Antioxidant effect of honey samples
sec.p: Free radicals contribute to the development of numerous chronic and degenerative diseases, therefore inclusion of antioxidant compounds in the diet is recommended to reduce oxidative damage [46, 47]. ABTS and DPPH assays are widely used as reliable methods for evaluating the total antioxidant capacity of honey, as they provide insight into the collective activity of its antioxidant constituents, such as polyphenols, flavonoids, and phenolic acids [47]. In our study, all analyzed natural honey samples exhibited antioxidant activity. Comparison between the tested honey samples revealed that, according to the DPPH assay, the highest radical scavenging capacity was observed in HH and MH, while the lowest in WCH. In contrast, the ABTS assay revealed that ACH, SH, and WCH exhibited the highest antioxidant activity. However, TRP showed the strongest performance in MH and HH. Likewise, the greatest TPC was recorded in dark honeys, such as HH and MH, compared to the lighter samples, where these concentrations were two to nearly four times lower, which aligns with other studies [48].

The antioxidant activity of honey reflects a synergistic interplay among polyphenols, flavonoids, ascorbic acid, amino acids, enzymes, and Maillard reaction products [48–51]. HH and MH samples, both darker and richer in phenolics, exhibited the highest activity in the DPPH and TRP assays, which is in line with previous observations that color intensity strongly correlates with polyphenol concentration and reducing capacity [48, 52].

Interestingly, the ABTS assay revealed greater activity in light honey varieties, suggesting that these samples may contain more hydrophilic antioxidants, such as ascorbic acid or specific phenolic acids (e.g., caffeic, ferulic) [48]. It is important to emphasize that antioxidant activity of tested honey samples can differ depending on the assay applied, as each method assesses different aspects of antioxidant mechanisms [50]. The divergence between DPPH and ABTS results underscores the complexity of honey’s redox behavior: DPPH mainly detects lipophilic radical scavengers, whereas ABTS also responds to hydrophilic ones [50, 53–55]. Consequently, antioxidant ranking depends not only on TPC [54, 56, 57], but also on the chemical polarity and solubility of the antioxidant species.

Overall, the data confirmed a strong but non-linear relationship between TPC and antioxidant activity. Dark honeys (HH, MH) excelled in DPPH and TRP assays due to high levels of polyphenols and flavonoids, while lighter honeys (ACH, SH) performed better in ABTS, indicating the presence of alternative hydrophilic antioxidants. These results highlight that honey’s antioxidant power is multifactorial and assay-dependent, validating the need for multiple test systems to fully capture its antioxidant potential.

sec.title: Antigenotoxicity of honey samples
sec.p: DNA is a highly sensitive molecule that can be damaged by a wide range of endogenous and environmental factors. Reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are continuously produced as natural byproducts of cellular metabolic processes, represent a major source of oxidative stress and DNA damage. Inadequate repair of continuous DNA damage may disrupt genetic stability [58]. There is strong evidence for the antigenotoxic effects of honey, supported by numerous studies [10, 11, 59–61]. The protective properties of honey and other natural products against DNA damage are closely linked to their antioxidant potential, their role in preserving genomic stability, and their capacity to activate cellular repair systems [9, 62–64]. These effects are primarily determined by the complex interplay of various bioactive components, including phenolics, peptides, organic acids, enzymes, and other biologically active substances [59].

D. melanogaster shares genetic and metabolic characteristics with mammals and has low maintenance cost, so it is a good model for genotoxicity and antigenotoxicity testing. Among the various methods used to evaluate DNA integrity, the comet assay stands out as a rapid and reliable technique for estimating the antigenotoxic properties of different substances [64–66].

The DNA protective effect against oxidative damage induced by hydroxyl and peroxyl radicals, as well as the antigenotoxic effect of the tested honeys in third-instar larvae of D. melanogaster, assessed by the alkaline comet assay, have not been previously reported. Only one study has investigated the potential DNA-protective effect of honey-sweetened cashew apple nectar against EMS- and mitomycin C-induced somatic mutation and recombination in D. melanogaster using the wing spot test [67]. Additionally, the in vivo DNA-protective potential of various honey types has been demonstrated in different model organisms using the comet assay [9].

All tested honey samples in our study demonstrated a significant in vitro protective effect against DNA damage induced by both hydroxyl and peroxyl radicals. A slight decrease in the protective effects was noted with samples’ increasing concentrations, which can be explained in one of the following ways:

list-item.p: Honey is a complex mixture in which some bioactive substances, such as polyphenols, at higher concentrations (in increased honey concentrations) can act prooxidatively, for example in combination with metal ions, when they can also create ROS [68, 69].

Known as a viscous liquid [70], honey at higher concentrations can increase viscosity of the medium and limit the diffusion of antioxidants toward DNA, reducing their effective concentration at the site of action.

sec.p: The in vivo DNA-protective activity of the tested honey samples ranked in the following decreasing order: ACH > MH > HH > SH > WCH. Honey samples ACH, MH, and HH at 20% concentration had the highest DNA-protective effects, showing percentage reductions of 91.76%, 84.24%, and 83.25%. Notably, even at lower concentrations, all tested natural honeys achieved greater than 50% reduction in EMS-induced DNA damage. High TPC and antioxidant activity of natural products have a significant impact on their antigenotoxic properties [71]. Interestingly, although TPC was the highest in HH and MH, ACH demonstrated the greatest antigenotoxic in vivo activity in our research. These results suggest that TPC alone may not be a reliable predictor of honey’s genoprotective potential, as interactions between TPC and other honey components can shift the phenolic profile from antioxidant to prooxidant [10, 48]. Likewise, according to ABTS assay, ACH exhibited superior radical scavenging activity compared to all other samples. Considering that ABTS assay covers a broader spectrum of reactive species [72] than DPPH, this may be one of the reasons why ACH has a stronger in vivo genoprotective effect in comparison with the other honey samples.

In addition, it has been stated that sugars also have an antimutagenic effect. Generally, monosaccharides inactivate mutagens before they are incorporated into the cell, and also interact with enzymes, catalyzing the metabolic activity of promutagens and interfering with the production of genotoxic intermediates. Glucose and fructose display considerably stronger effects than disaccharides like maltose and sucrose [73]. In our study, ACH and SH were found to contain elevated amounts of glucose and fructose relative to the other tested honeys. The high glucose and fructose content, combined with increased values ​​of other mentioned parameters in ACH, could partially explain the strongest in vivo antigenotoxic effects of this honey sample. Nevertheless, the HH and MH samples demonstrated antigenotoxic effects only slightly lower than those of ACH, which can be attributed to their strong antioxidant activity (DPPH assay) and high TPC level.

sec.title: Antimicrobial effect of honey samples
sec.p: The antimicrobial properties of honey are well documented. It has been traditionally used for treating infectious diseases [13], and preclinical and clinical studies confirm its efficacy [14, 74–76]. The possible prebiotic effect of honey on probiotic bacteria in the microbiome may also contribute to its antimicrobial efficacy in therapeutic applications [77]. However, honey’s antimicrobial potential varies greatly between samples [67]. Moreover, methodological approaches used to assess antimicrobial activity, as well as the microbial strains chosen for testing, can significantly affect results [78]. Multiple physicochemical parameters have been associated with honey’s antimicrobial properties: acidity and low pH (typically 3.2–6.1), high sugar content (~ 80% by weight), low water activity, and production of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) [79, 80]. Additionally, the presence of phenolic and flavonoid compounds, peptides and proteins, and unique components such as methylglyoxal (MGO) and bee defensin-1 play a role in honey’s antimicrobial mechanisms [81–84].

In our study, considerable differences were observed in the antimicrobial properties of the tested honey samples. According to the classification proposed by Romário-Silva et al. [85], which is based on MIC values (strong: 1.0–12.5%, moderate: 12.5–50.0%, weak: >50.0%), the MH sample could be classified as a honey sample with strong antimicrobial activity. It demonstrated MIC values ranging from 6.3% to 12.5% against S. aureus and all tested Gram-negative bacteria. This sample also had high TPC, the highest TRP, strong DPPH radical scavenging activity, and the highest acidity among the tested honeys. All these parameters probably contributed to its strong antimicrobial properties. The HH sample with the highest TPC value and the best DPPH activity showed good antibacterial activity against S. aureus and all tested Gram-negative bacteria with MIC values between 12.5% and 25.0%. Our results are comparable with those obtained by similar studies [63, 86], with the exception that, in our case, MH showed slightly superior properties compared to HH, indicating that local environmental conditions have a significant influence on characteristics of honeys, even within the same type.

The better antimicrobial effect of honey on bacteria compared to yeasts, as well as its greater efficacy against Gram-negative bacteria than Gram-positive bacteria, has been demonstrated in many studies [74, 87–89]. In our study, En. faecalis and C. albicans exhibited the highest resistance among all tested strains, whereas Gram-negative bacteria were generally more sensitive than Gram-positive. The observed greater susceptibility of Gram-negative bacteria, compared to Gram-positive bacteria, may result from structural differences and distinct stress responses between these two bacterial groups. Studies on the inhibitory mechanisms of manuka honey against S. aureus and P. aeruginosa have shown that these mechanisms are entirely different, involving the activation of distinct stress response genes [90]. The lower susceptibility of En. faecalis to the inhibitory activity of honey may be due to its strong ability to adapt to stressful conditions, particularly acidic and osmotic stress, which are recognized as important factors in the antimicrobial mechanism of honey [91, 92]. On the other hand, C. albicans, as a eukaryotic organism, has a more complex cell wall structure than bacteria [93]. Its cell wall is primarily composed of β-1,3-glucan, with smaller amounts of β-1,6-glucan and chitin, which may contribute to its greater resistance to the various stress factors present in honey. P. paraeruginosa was the most susceptible strain, showing the lowest MIC values across all honey samples. Similar patterns were reported by Gregorio et al. [94], where honeys from five regions in Brazil showed consistent activity against S. aureus, E. coli, and C. albicans, while yeasts exhibited the highest resistance.

Honey’s pH plays a significant role in microbial inhibition [95]. In our samples, pH ranged from 4.18 (SH) to 5.06 (WCH), values that are unfavorable for most microorganisms, which typically grow at neutral pH levels (6.5–7.5) [13]. Furthermore, the high sugar content (> 80% in all samples except MH) creates a hypertonic environment that inhibits microbial growth by drawing water from bacterial cells through the process of osmosis [81, 96, 97]. WCH and ACH samples had the highest glucose content, which may enhance antibacterial activity upon dilution by increasing H₂O₂ production through the enzymatic glucose oxidation [98], contributing to their moderate antimicrobial potential.

The dry matter and ash content of honey can also influence its antimicrobial activity. Samples with high dry matter content, mainly due to high sugar concentration, inhibit microbial growth through increased osmotic pressure [13, 84]. The MH sample, which showed the strongest antimicrobial activity, also had the highest dry matter content among the tested samples. This may contribute, along with its other antimicrobial properties, to its overall antimicrobial potential. Ash content, representing the inorganic residues remaining after the carbonisation of honey, can indirectly affect antimicrobial activity by influencing the honey’s electrical conductivity and stability [99, 100]. The HH and ACH samples had the highest ash content, which may enhance their antimicrobial potential.

The antimicrobial effects of the tested honey samples cannot be attributed to any single factor, but rather to the complex interplay among various physicochemical properties and bioactive components. Environmental factors, including floral and honeydew diversity play a significant role in shaping the observed antimicrobial profiles.

Taken together, the results of this study indicate that different types of honey may exert beneficial effects on human health due to their diverse bioactive constituents. However, monofloral honeys, due to their more consistent chemical profiles, may provide more predictable health-promoting effects compared to polyfloral honeys. Likewise, it is very important to emphasize that the therapeutic application of honey should also consider dose adjustment, as bioactive efficacy is dose-dependent and may vary among different honey types.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The results of investigation confirm that presented honey samples have strong antioxidant, DNA-protective, and antimicrobial properties, supporting their potential therapeutic value. The combined data indicate that no single honey type dominates across all parameters: Honeydew and Meadow honeys are the most potent antioxidants and possess strong antimicrobial properties, Acacia honey shows exceptional DNA-protective potential while Sunflower honey demonstrates solid ABTS activity and antifungal effects.

These are important findings, given that Acacia honey is one of the most valued monofloral honeys, while Honeydew and polyfloral honeys such as Meadow honey are traditionally appreciated for their quality. Likewise, presented results underscore the importance of honey’s botanical and honeydew origin in defining its bioactivity. Future work should integrate advanced chromatographic and spectroscopic profiling to identify individual phenolics, flavonoids, and sugars responsible for these activities, providing a deeper mechanistic understanding of honey’s health benefits.
